practice1.prompt: Write count_down(n) recursively: print n, then n-1, down to 1, then "Done!". Call it with 5.

cases.name: counts down from 5 and then stops
count_down is a function that takes the number to count from
cases.describe: a function count_down(n) that takes one argument

cases.name: there is a base case
cases.describe: an if that stops the recursion when the number runs out

cases.name: each call is made on a smaller number
cases.describe: the next call made with a smaller number, like count_down(n - 1)

cases.name: the counting is done by recursion, not by a loop
cases.describe: count_down calling itself, with no for or while doing the counting

practice1.hint: A while loop that prints and decrements gives the same output, so the output alone cannot tell the two apart. Ask what makes the second number get printed: another call, or another turn of a loop.

questions.prompt: What happens if a recursive function has no base case?
choices: It calls itself until Python gives up and raises RecursionError
questions.explain: Nothing stops the descent, so each call makes another call. Python caps the depth and raises RecursionError rather than running out of memory.

questions.prompt: In the lesson's factorial, what does factorial(0) return?
questions.explain: 0 and 1 are the base cases and both return 1. That is what lets factorial(5) finish: the chain of multiplications has something to end on.

questions.prompt: Every recursive function needs a ___ case that stops it, and a ___ case that calls itself with a smaller problem.
questions.explain: The base case is the smallest version of the problem, solved directly. The recursive case is the step that gets closer to it.

questions.prompt: Put these lines in order so the function adds up a list recursively.
questions.explain: The base case comes first so an empty list returns before anything is indexed. numbers[0] on an empty list would raise IndexError.

questions.prompt: Which of these problems fit recursion well?
choices: Adding up a list of prices
questions.explain: Trees, divide-and-conquer and backtracking are recursive in shape, so the code follows the shape. Adding up a flat list is a single pass, and a loop says that more plainly.

reflection-exercise2.hint: Say what a recursive call does to the size of the problem, then give one concrete problem it works on.
